beats.narration_text: Ahoj — I'm Vedanshu Daxesh Patel. Chapter one ended on one sentence: the model never saw the document. This film takes that sentence apart — three separate failures hiding inside it, and why the easy fix, a bigger context window, doesn't touch any of them.

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole shape of it: 'not enough information' is really three unrelated failures — what the model invents, what it never learned had changed, and what it's handed but can't use well. Each needs its own fix. None of them is one bigger box.

beats.narration_text: Picture the help-desk assistant chapter one introduced: an employee, a question typed into a chat window, and a model about to answer with whatever it has — no lookup, no second source, just what it already holds.

beats.narration_text: Zoom into that window. A cursor blinks after the question. Whatever comes back next will read exactly as confident whether it's right or wrong — that's the trap this whole film is about.

a soft glow suggests a response about to appear

beats.narration_text: Three ways that answer can go wrong, and this film takes each one in turn: confident invention, frozen memory, and a fact that's there but never found. Then the harder question — why making the window bigger doesn't fix any of them.

chip 2 lands: Stale Knowledge

beats.narration_text: Act two: hallucination — the first way a fluent answer can be completely wrong.

'Confident, Wrong' title types in

beats.narration_text: There's an old stage trick that captures this exactly: reach into an empty hat, and something specific and convincing comes out anyway. That's what a model does when it's asked something it was never told.

show.event: wide shot: a magician's hands over an empty hat, stage light

shot.prompt: Tier 1 (generic, no real referent). See SHOPPING.md.

beats.narration_text: Watch the hand, not the hat. Whatever comes out arrives with total confidence — no hesitation, no disclaimer. That confidence is the whole problem: it looks identical to actually knowing.

show.event: tight shot on the object being pulled out, confident flourish
spotlight holds; nothing marks the object as invented

shot.prompt: Tier 1 (generic, no real referent) — same plate/family as B06. See SHOPPING.md.

beats.narration_text: Researchers split this into two flavors. Intrinsic: the answer flatly contradicts a real source. Extrinsic: there's no source to check it against at all. Both read exactly as confident as a correct answer would.

show.event: question node splits into two labeled paths
'intrinsic — contradicts a source' and 'extrinsic — no source to check' labels settle
citation line fades in

production_viz.label: intrinsic vs. extrinsic hallucination
production_viz.mechanic: question node branches into two labeled outcome boxes
production_viz.note: Ji et al. 2023; Huang et al. 2023 — no invented rate

beats.narration_text: Ask about a benefit the company never offered, and the model doesn't pause — it invents specific, plausible terms, because plausible-sounding text is exactly what it was trained to produce.

show.event: 'Hallucination' headline types in
empty, greyed-out source shelf appears
confident answer bubble writes itself, no citation stamp
spark line settles: confident ≠ correct

props.headline: Hallucination
props.detail: Intrinsic vs. extrinsic — both read equally confident (Ji et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2023).

beats.narration_text: Grounding a model in real documents helps — human evaluation shows it measurably reduces hallucination in conversation. But the researchers who showed this were careful: a reduction, never an elimination. The curve bends down. It doesn't reach zero.

curve flattens above the zero line — never reaching it
'reduction, not elimination' label + citation

production_viz.label: grounding reduces, doesn't eliminate, hallucination
production_viz.note: Shuster et al. 2021 — no invented rate number on screen

beats.narration_text: Act three: stale knowledge. Somewhere in an archive, a shelf of records sits exactly as it was the day it was last touched — nothing added, nothing corrected, no matter how much time has passed outside.

show.event: wide shot: dusty archive shelves, stacks of old bound documents, light through a high window
slow push toward one stack

shot.prompt: Tier 1 (generic, no real referent). See SHOPPING.md.

beats.narration_text: This is exactly how these models are built: train once on a fixed snapshot, deploy, and stop. No further learning happens while the world keeps changing underneath. Vendor reports state this outright — a cutoff, by design, not by accident.

show.event: 'train' tick, then 'deploy' tick on a timeline
a second line for 'the world' keeps moving past deploy; the model's line stops
'frozen the moment training stops' label + citation

production_viz.label: train once, deploy, stop learning
production_viz.mechanic: two timelines, one stopping, one continuing
production_viz.note: OpenAI, 2023 — no specific cutoff date stated

beats.narration_text: Ask about a benefit that was discontinued last year, and a model trained before the change describes the old terms as current — fluently, with no internal flag saying anything might be out of date.

show.event: status indicator reads 'current'
a 'policy changed' marker passes by, off to the side, unnoticed
indicator still reads 'current' — no flag trips

production_viz.label: no internal staleness flag
production_viz.mechanic: a status indicator that never updates as a marker passes it
production_viz.note: matches the chapter's own worked example — no invented dates beyond its framing

beats.narration_text: It doesn't know what it doesn't know. The policy chip flips from current to retired the moment it crosses the cutoff — and the model on the near side of that line never sees it happen.

show.event: timeline draws with a cutoff marker
policy chip flips from 'current' to 'retired'
spark line settles: it doesn't know what it doesn't know

beats.narration_text: Act four: context limits — the failure that survives even when nothing is missing and nothing has gone stale.

show.event: 'ACT IV' kicker fades in
terracotta rule draws
'Lost In The Middle' title types in

beats.narration_text: Picture a desk buried under one long document — every page technically there, every fact technically included, and the one paragraph that actually answers the question sitting somewhere in the middle of all of it.

show.event: wide shot: a desk buried under a single long unrolled document / stacked pages
slow push toward the middle of the pile

shot.prompt: Tier 1 (generic, no real referent). See SHOPPING.md.

beats.narration_text: Every request has a hard ceiling on how much text it can hold — prompt and output combined. That ceiling has grown across model generations, but it has never disappeared, and it never fully will.

show.event: three generation columns appear, each with its own ceiling line
each column's fill rises toward its own ceiling, never past it
'bigger each generation — never unbounded' label + citation

production_viz.label: bounded, ever-growing context window
production_viz.mechanic: three columns, each with a hard ceiling line at a different height
production_viz.note: OpenAI, 2023 — no specific token count stated

beats.narration_text: Size alone doesn't save you. Research on long-context use found accuracy highest when the answer sits at the very start or end of the input — and it drops hard when that same fact is buried in the middle, even when everything fits.

show.event: a long bar fills in, bright at both ends
the middle segment dims progressively
start/middle/end labels settle + citation, ordering only, no numbers

production_viz.label: lost in the middle — qualitative ordering
production_viz.mechanic: a segmented bar bright at the edges, dim in the middle
production_viz.note: Liu et al., 2024 — ordering only, no accuracy figures invented

beats.narration_text: Fits is not the same as used. The fact can be sitting right there in the pasted context and still never get the weight it needs to actually answer the question.

show.event: Start/Middle/End markers appear
Start and End bars rise; Middle bar dips
caption settles: fits ≠ used

beats.act: V — Necessary For Some, Useless For Others
beats.narration_text: Act five: it's tempting to treat all three as one problem with one fix — just make the window bigger. Here's what that fix actually looks like: a much bigger container, and exactly the same amount of anything useful inside it.

show.event: wide shot: an oversized empty suitcase or moving box, lid open, cavernous
slow push into the empty interior

shot.prompt: Tier 1 (generic, no real referent). See SHOPPING.md.

beats.act: V — Necessary For Some, Useless For Others
beats.narration_text: Watch the box grow. Doubling, tripling in size changes nothing about whether the one lost item inside it gets found — the box's size was never what determined that. A bigger window doesn't stop hallucination, doesn't fix stale training data, and doesn't guarantee the right passage gets used either.

production_viz.mechanic: a box scaling up while a marked lost item inside stays unfound
production_viz.note: no invented numbers — a pure size/outcome-independence metaphor

beats.narration_text: Three separate lines, one direction: what's invented, what's gone stale, and what's buried all trace back to the same missing step — deciding what the model actually sees. That decision has a name. Chapter three starts there.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap the whole film. Hallucination, stale knowledge, and context limits are three different failures, not three symptoms of one. A bigger window fixes none of them by itself — necessary for some problems, useless for others. What they share is a missing step: deciding, at the moment of the question, which small part of everything available actually answers it. That's not a bigger box. That's a different mechanism, and it's where chapter three begins.

artifactLines: Hallucination: confident, invented answers — grounding in real documents helps, but doesn't guarantee only true output (Shuster et al., 2021).
Stale knowledge: frozen at the training cutoff, with no internal flag for what's since changed (OpenAI, 2023).
Context limits: a hard token ceiling, and the 'lost in the middle' effect — a fact can fit and still get ignored depending on where it sits (Liu et al., 2024).
A bigger window fixes none of these alone — the shared missing step is deciding which passage matters, at question-time. Chapter three names that decision.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: 'I have a document I rely on for answers — using the three failure modes from this film, walk me through where you'd invent an answer if you'd never seen part of it, where your knowledge might already be out of date, and if I handed you the whole thing at once, where in it would the important fact most likely get lost?' Run it on something you actually rely on, and watch which of the three Claude actually names for your document.
